utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did have an application, but upon my client's specific instructions I no longer have an application to make this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Musliu wishes to stay in court to hear this witness. Thank you for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With full attendance, we can mark the roll and carry on. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness and, Your Honours, may be glad to know the last witness for -- live witness for Mr. Limaj is Fadil Bajraktari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please read allowed the affirmation on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to receive a translation of what I'm saying to you? There seems to be an issue there. Could that be attended to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is okay. I receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have a translation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, now I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mansfield, you're on air.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Mr. Mansfield:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bajraktari, I'm over here. I represent Mr. Fatmir Limaj who is sitting behind me. I speak slowly because there is an interpreter, and if you could do the same. It is easier in that manner.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a series of questions. I'll take them in chronological order. First of all, is it right that you were born in 1974?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us where you were born?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: I was born in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you always lived in Pristina since that time?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: No, no. I have lived in my village in Kishna Reka, Drenas municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for how long did you live in that -- have you lived in that village?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: In Pristina I started to live after 1994, whereas in the village I lived from -- since when I was a child until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a little about the situation in 1998. What was your work at that time?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: At the time, I was a student at the faculty of philology, Albanian literature and language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you do any work as a journalist at all?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: No. Not in 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start doing work as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: I started work as a journalist in 1999 after the establishment of Kosova Press news agency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about, therefore, the time before that when you were, in 1998, forced to live in the mountains. That's what -- the period I want to ask about. First of all, when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes. After the massacres that occurred in Likoshan, Qirez, and then in Prekaz, I was in Pristina. I returned to my village to stay with my family and to follow the reality that was created at that time. And ever since, after the war, I remained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many members of your family were there?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: We were an extended family, because after the outbreak of the war, my sisters who were married and were living elsewhere came and joined us to the village because they felt safer there. So we had children, only children we had 14 beginning from the age of 11, children of my brothers and sisters. It was rather hard for us to cope.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you just describe, before we get to the meeting with Fatmir Limaj, can you just describe the conditions under which yourself and your family were living?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: You want to know the conditions after we went to the mountains?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Okay. The conditions of my family were the same as those of the other citizens who had taken to the mountains. They were very difficult indeed. It was a miserable situation for all of us, and we didn't know whether we would be able to make it for the next day. We were living in some makeshift places using some timber, some nylon tents. It was there we stayed, prepared our food. It was in good and in bad weather we were staying there. When we went to the mountains it was August, September and November. During that time we remained there. And in September, October, and early November the weather worsens. Sometimes it even snows. The weather conditions and all the conditions in general were very difficult, but they were more so for the children, because you can imagine children were very young until 11 years old. The eldest of them was my nephew. So for them it was very hard. If you want to have a realistic idea of what we went through, I have a picture of my nephew who was born in the month of May of 1999, and due to lack of food and proper hygienic conditions for a baby to grow up, you can see in the picture I have for yourselves what Your Honours think it would be a proper idea of showing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just for the moment if you -- we already have some photographs. If you can just describe the condition of that particular child you obviously have in mind. Just describe it, if you wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: The condition of that small baby was very difficult. He lacked foodstuffs. He left -- he missed everything for a normal life. Just a fact. He was born over four kilos, and in the seventh month of his life he weighed 1.7 kilogrammes. So you can imagine being born four kilogrammes when he was seven months old, he was only 1.7 kilogrammes. He was only a heap of bones, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to come to the time when you met Fatmir Limaj. Do you remember, first of all, when that was roughly?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes. Roughly it was by the mid-September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: That was in the valley of our village where the population had taken shelter. That is in the valley of Kishna Reka village. It is situated or it is next to the Berisha Mountains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you give Their Honours a rough idea of how many people we're dealing with here that were sheltering in that way?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: We are talking about 1998. There were, I believe, over 4.000 only in that valley. I mean, inhabitants of our village and of some other villages who had fled from their respective villages. They were from Orlat, Terpeze and other villages, and they had taken shelter there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, had you ever met Fatmir Limaj before that time that you met him?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just describe the situation of the meeting. What happened?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: When he first came, I didn't see him, but I saw him when he was talking with some villagers. He was with some other soldiers. Out of curiosity, I went near to see what they were talking about. What made me join the talk, the conversation, with Fatmir, whose name I didn't know and who I didn't know other than as a soldier of the KLA - that was the impression he gave me from his look and from his conversation - I was impressed at the way he looked at the children who were barefooted. It was the spring nearby. It was a muddy place. You can imagine because of the water flowing it was a muddy place and the children were walking barefoot. So I felt very sad looking at the children and the villagers, seeing in what conditions they were living, and I saw that he shared the same sadness. I could see it in his look. I started to talk with him after some conversations we had in which he showed an interest in the conditions of the villagers who were living in, whether they had food, whether they had clothes to wear, how they were living. He asked me whether there were people with higher education there, and I said yes, and then, "Why are you asking me?" And then he replied, "Because it would be a good idea if we could organise some sort of education for the children even though we don't have the conditions for a proper school and education, but in this way at least the children would have a place to go and something to do other than just live in dread of being shelled and killed. So during part of the day they can learn something."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened about this idea that he spoke about with you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: That was a very good idea in fact, an idea which I really liked. So I asked him, "What shall we do?" And he promised me to see if he could find some possibilities of providing us with some book -- books, some pencils, some notebooks or something else. After three or four days, the people there built the school -- school, a makeshift school, actually, with whatever we could have there, and we received notebooks and pencils for the children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what role did you play, if any, in this? What did you do yourself?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: My role in all this was that of a teacher. I taught the kids.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Fatmir again about these matters on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: I didn't see him for the -- this particular topic, that is to talk about the school and the teaching, but -- but when I saw him I asked him, "What are we going to do? We don't have any curricula. Do you have any ideas?" And then he said, "Yes. You must teach them as much as you can in these circumstances from the books you have, but should pay special attention to keep them busy and divert their attention from the fear of death," which was a constant fear with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time were there attacks by the Serbs nearby which you could hear or see?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes. At that time all the time we were staying there there were constant attacks. There was constant shelling, because we were in the valley. So it was only shelling that could reach us or close to us. It wasn't light gunfire that could reach us. We were never calm because of that situation. I have a CD here. I have recorded something from that time about the conditions where we lived and how we lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Fatmir ever come and visit the school once it was up and running and speak to you or the pupils there?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes, he did come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us a bit about that, please.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: He came a few days after we had started our lessons. He said he was sorry to intervene in the lesson, but he said he wanted to know how the lessons were going and how the children were doing. But we welcomed him. We were very happy he was there. Not only him but we welcomed any other soldier of the KLA. The children were distressed and their conditions were very bad, so whoever came to visit us, we considered that a great contribution because the children could see that there are soldiers who can protect us and the Serbs cannot do anything to us. It was important for him to speak to them and give them hope and help them, and help them get their fear [as interpreted] of the Serbs and of death. The children had seen on television about what the Serbs had done, so the children had created an idea that if the Serbs would come, they would kill them immediately. At the same time, they had heard about the Delijaj massacre in Obrinje, and I think they had seen some photographs that a journalist, an American journalist had made. Among the victims in the photographs there was a two-year-old child, so the children were terribly scared. And they were scared -- they feared that they would have the same fate if the Serbs came. Then the -- then Fatmir spoke with me. He asked me about the conditions, where the children were living and studying, and whether the children were getting used to the idea that they would have lessons every day, whether they were forgetting about this fear. He smiled to the children, and that was important. He was very polite to them and to me. He apologised for intervening and then he left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you dealt with obviously fear, protection, education. I just want to ask you about food. Did he help with that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: The situation was very difficult because the citizens had left their homes unprepared. They had taken what they could at the moment because the Serb offensive that August morning, it was a very swift action on the part of the Serbs. The morning was very foggy. It was very early morning. We couldn't see anything that morning. Only when we heard the shelling coming towards us the villagers understood that they were surrounded. So you can imagine -- you can imagine what could the villagers take in half an hour while the developing was going on. So the food situation was very, very difficult, because it was also the beginning for us, and the citizens did not know what they had to take with themselves. They didn't know for how long they would stay in the mountains, whether they would be in the mountains for a long time or whether the Serb forces would come there and chase them away. So this was the situation. They did not think of anything else, no luxuries. They only wanted a piece of bread. That's what they wanted, just to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of how Fatmir helped with the basic commodities?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes. This is still the period of August 1998. In September, as I told you, Fatmir showed his interest about our situation, and a few days later some food came on a lorry. There was pasta, food, some sugar and salt. And Fatmir said, "This is all I can do. I can't do more about these people here." People lived in those mountains and valleys all through 1999, and later there was better organisation on the part of the KLA because during winter months they had collected food supplies for the citizens and the villagers in order for them to be well supplied during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you just briefly to look at some photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honours have this series of photographs. I think there are six. If you could just -- yes. If these photographs could be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just ask which batch those are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It's the last batch, and I think its 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one is a photograph of me. It was made -- it was taken in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that it's on the -- sorry, it has to be recorded. So this one is in fact, I think, numbered photograph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And Your Honours have it at the top of the first sheet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's photograph 1. And now would you go to photograph 2. It's on the bottom of the first page of the photocopy. Can you just describe what this is?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photograph that I took. Sorry, it was a photograph taken by a reporter of the TVSH, which is the Albanian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. television. It is the photograph of the school. This is a photograph that was taken before the lesson started. This is the school. This is the place where the lessons were held. There were only two classes that we organised, one on the left and one on the right. There were more children than there are here in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many children were you teaching?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: There were 300 pupils in that school more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can we see you, in fact, in this photograph? Are you pictured in it?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes, in other pictures, not here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you go to the next one, number 3?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the top of our second page. Can you describe this scene to us, please.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: This photograph shows part of the place where the citizens lived. You can see it's a makeshift place where they lived. The conditions were very, very difficult. You can see there's a nylon tent here where the people lived. Where the child is you can see that place. There's a source of water where we got our water from. It was very muddy here, so not many people lived in this particular place. It's only a corner of the area where the people lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you put up, please, number 4, which is at the bottom of the second page.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: So this is the other photograph. It's again part of the place where the citizens lived. You can see that there are more tents here, so more people lived here. Look at the children. That's what they did all about, moving about in the mud here. And the idea to have them organised in some kind of school was a very good idea. I still get emotional now when I think about it, because there were so many children who came to that school. These children now are seven or eight -- seven years older, and now they live in good conditions. And they still remember me, and they call me the teacher of the mountains, and they hug me whenever they see me. And it was Fatmir's idea for me to become the teacher of the mountains. So this is his humane spirit. He has a grand spirit, a humane spirit. He was great.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, photograph number 5 on the last page of our photocopy, please.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: This is a picture that was taken during the lesson. This is one corner of the classroom, if we can call it so. The children were sitting on some logs. They have some notebooks. These are the notebooks and the pencils that Fatmir promised us, and they arrived a few days later I've talked to him. Because these children, when they left their homes, they did not anything. They did not have these notebooks or pencils, nor did they have anything else, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just was checking -- yes. Are you in the photograph itself? Are you the person who is standing --

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes, it's me. And I have here with me a newspaper, and that newspaper contains a similar photograph to this. There is an article in that newspaper that describes the conditions in which we held those lessons. In order to reinforce what this photograph shows, that's what I mean, if you want to look at it. I've got also a recording that a cameraman did at that time. In addition to working in this school, I also worked in the people's tents where they lived with the children there. I went to a pupil there whose brother -- whose brother had been killed. We tried to work with her because she was distressed. You know, her brother was only 20 years old, so she was distressed. And we tried with all our efforts. We did our best to support those children. We tried to make them socialise. We tried to help them have the will and the desire to help each other and not wait only for my word or my advice to do things. These children now have overcome their traumas, and I think what they -- what we did at that period of time helped them overcome their traumas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to just move a little towards the end of 1998 and, in particular, do you have a recollection about a particular grenade attack that occurred? Yes, at or near the school.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just describe what happened and obviously any connection to Fatmir Limaj there is.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes. Before I start to describe it, I would like to say that the idea that those children could be killed by a shell, that was a fear I had all the time. The children could have been killed in their places where they lived, in their tents, because the enemy shelled everywhere, because they did it indiscriminately. I can remember one moment when the shelling started, and it was very heavy shelling close to the school, and I told the children to leave the school and go somewhere that was safer. Fatmir and some soldiers were passing by that area at the time. Fatmir had -- Fatmir took two or three children with himself and told the other children also to follow him and go down the valley because it would be safer there. And I still have that emotional feeling and experience here with me today. I still feel that he had a great heart, a humane spirit, a humane soul who thought about those children. Fatmir could have continued with his -- with what he was doing, going to the fighting, wherever he was going, but he stopped for the children and stayed with them during the time of the shelling. And he told them, "When the shelling starts, you should not stand. You should lie down, because the shelling is very dangerous when you stand." These are small things, but he helped them a lot. He helped me a lot as well, because these pieces of advice that he gave, it was a great support for me as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have only one more question and it really links to that last point. What difference has Fatmir made to your life? Not just the children but to you personally.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BAJRAKTARI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. He has influenced my life a lot. I want to go back to an earlier period. In March of 1998, I was very sick. I had a kidney problem. I was in Pristina, and I went back to my village. The doctor I saw for my problem was Lutfi Dervishi, and he proposed me to have an operation in order to become well again. The situation in that hospital was not good. The conditions were almost horrible, so this operation remained an idea. So in those very difficult moments, I decided to go to my village. I wanted to be close to my family, where I belonged. So also when, we went to the mountains, I was feeling worse and worse. A medical team came from the Red Cross, from Geneva, and they took me -- they wanted to take me abroad to be cured, but Fatmir's idea to have a school to teach the children made me refuse that idea. I told those doctors that I won't come. I decided to stay with the children. I proposed them to take two young mothers who were about to give birth. I couldn't leave those children there even if I would feel well again and my kidneys would become better. I did not want that life. I wanted to be close to the children because my life was with them. Believe me, the miracle happened. I did not go to the doctor again. I did not need that surgery any more. The kidney stones that I had, I passed them out by myself until February 1999. So I did not need the surgery any more. That's what happened to me. And today I'm fit as a fiddle. I don't suffer any more. But it was Fatmir who taught me how to become a teacher, to become a teacher of those children, "The teacher of the mountain," as they called me. I would like to describe, too, one early experience of mine. When I was in the eighth grade, there was a protest of the citizens and the Serb forces started to shoot against the crowd. I'm speaking now about 1989 when the constitutional changes were happening in Yugoslavia. So the Serbs were shooting and three citizens were killed. Several others were injured. That was my first trauma as a child. That was the first time when the idea occurred to me that we could be dead at any moment. Whether I was a child or whether I was an adult person, they would shoot at you and kill you. So that's what helped me find the force and the energy within myself to be close to the children later on. I never hesitated to stop and talk to the children whether it was at the water spring or whether it was at their tents or in the school. That was a very difficult period for all the citizens until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could -- I wonder if Your Honours would permit the photographs to be an exhibit themselves, the original photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Defence Exhibit DL16, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How many are there altogether?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Five. Five.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The five photographs will be DL16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Will you wait there please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bajraktari, thank you very much for coming. That concludes the evidence that has been given by you in support of Mr. Limaj, and you are now, of course, free to return to your home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter would like the witness to say that again. Sorry. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we can leave it. It was a farewell greeting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes the case for Fatmir Limaj, save for four statements to which the Prosecution kindly have no objection to be tendered under the 92 bis regulation. And once the formalities have been completed, we would ask that those four statements, the last one of which was mentioned only the other day, that's the military officer called Clark, and obviously subject to the order of Your Honour's Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you are tendering in anticipation to create another legal concept four statements by consent, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Right. They will be received, and they will be given numbers when they are avail be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm most grateful. There is one other rider only, and that is it arises out of the statement of Mr. Clark, the last of the four. I think we have already indicated that we have sent that to Mr. Churcher who gave evidence here who may or may not have anything to add and we might have to obviously ask if he has something to add to admit a supplemental statement, but that hasn't arisen yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, on that basis that is the close of your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Guy-Smith, you're -- things were speeded up a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We stand at the ready to commence on Tuesday if that is workable with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And your anticipation of length of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If all goes as anticipated, we believe that the case for Mr. Bala will conclude within the week, hopefully no later than Friday therefore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to ensure Mr. Topolski is on adequate notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He asks me constantly and I try to reassure him as much as I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. And are you in a position to indicate whether your client will be giving evidence at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He will -- at this point, I believe unless things change radically not be giving evidence. However, he has indicated that he does wish to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. In those circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm encouraged, Mr. Topolski, to make a very gentle inquiry whether you're in a position to indicate anything of the length of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Gentle inquiry will get a gentle response and a diplomatic one at the moment. That is in a state of fluidity, and I will know by 4.00 today much more than I know now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No need to say more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'd rather not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We are grateful if I could indicate, Mr. Mansfield, to your attention you've given to dealing with the essential issues and confining your case accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And clearly we need to adjourn now, and we'll resume on Tuesday at 2.15. In the meantime, the Chamber will give attention to the written motion that is before us and the submissions we have received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of June, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 9.51 a.m.,
